BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, animation foundations, 33 terms for making motion in Godot, from clips and tracks to tweens, bones, and headless checks. The exact term lets you tell an AI coding agent what to change and test that it really happened.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in For Bear. A newcomer usually thinks an animation is something a node does by itself. It is not. An animation is data, a length and tracks of keys, and nothing moves until an animation player plays it. Many of the terms ahead come in pairs that are easy to mix up. This film takes them group by group and shows each one at work.

BDEFS.heard: Eight labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Editor or docs, the term comes from the editor itself or its official documentation. Outside source, the term comes from a source outside the course text, computed. The numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured, conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 33 terms about making motion in Go-Doh and checking that it happens when you think in four groups. The first group is Clips and Players, the Animation Resource, Animation Player, Animation Library, and Animated Sprite 2D. It covers what holds the motion and what plays it.

B0102.heard: The second group is tracks and keys. Track key, play head and interpolation, then the value method Bezi A and audio tracks. These terms say what a clip is made of and how values are filled in between the stored points.

B0103.heard: The third group is Time and tweens. Loop mode, loop seems, speed scale, auto play, the animation finished signal, callback modes, update mode, tween, easing, transition type and kill. They say when things run, how fast and how code drives motion.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is Bones and Chex. Skeleton, Rest Pose, Inverse Kindmatics, Pole Target, Fabric, Look at, Skeleton IK3D, Skeleton Updated, Fixed Frame Rate and Backend Limit. They cover posing a body and what you can test headless with no window.

B0201.heard: A code box shows one clip named Attack Fast. An animation resource is stored animation data, a length plus tracks of keys. This one is 0.45 seconds long with a rotation track and a method track among its four. It is data not behavior so nothing moves until a player plays it. For example, a spinning coin in your game could be a single animation resource with one rotation track, saved in the coin's scene file.

B0202.heard: Now an animation player is joined to that clip. The animation player is the node that plays animations by name. It moves the playhead along the clip and the property follows, so at 0.45 seconds the blade's rotation is 75 degrees. The animation is the data, and the animation player is the node that plays it. For example, the Walker Sword scene has its own animation player node. And the sword script tells it which attack clip to play on each swing of the combo.

B0203.heard: A box of five names is linked to one clip. An animation library is a name collection of animations that a player holds. It maps each name to an animation resource and calling play with a name picks one. Here the name attack fast picks a clip 0.45 seconds long. For example, the Walker Sords animation player holds five animations among them idle, attack fast and attack medium, so the combo code only has to ask for a name.

B0204.heard: Two ways to play a sprite sheet. An animated sprite 2D is a 2D node that plays a list of frames and that is all it does. In this made-up example it shows four frames at eight frames per second, half a second per cycle. An animation player can key the frame 2 and also position and monitoring on one timeline. For example, a coin that just flips through four drawings fits an animated sprite 2D. But an attack whose hitbox must switch on with a frame needs an animation player.

B0301.heard: An empty chart labeled with one property, rotation degrees. A track holds one property's keyframes inside a clip, bound to a node path. One track means one property on one node, and its keys will sit on this line between zero and 0.45 seconds. For example, if your player's jump clip should both squash the sprite and lift it, that takes two tracks, one for its scale, and one for its position.

B0302.heard: Three red dots sit on the track. A key is one point on a track holding a time, a value, and an easing value. This sword track has three minus 80 degrees at zero, 85 degrees at zero point one five seconds and 75 at zero point two. A key is a stored point, not the place the clip has reached. For example, a door in your level needs two keys on its rotation track, shut at the start, and open at the end.

B0303.heard: A red line sweeps across the track. The playhead is the marker for the current time on the timeline. The engine looks up the track at that time and sets the property, so at 0.45 seconds the rotation is 75 degrees. Key stay put and the playhead moves. For example, when you drag along a clip's timeline in the Godot editor to check a jump pose, you are moving the playhead by hand.

B0304.heard: Three lines now join the same keys. Interpolation is how the values between keys are filled in. Nearest takes the value of the closest key. Linear draws a straight line and cubic bends a smooth curve. At 0.06 seconds, they give minus 80, minus 14, and minus 17.5 degrees. For example, a pixel art arm that should snap from pose to pose wants nearest, while a camera that glides wants linear or cubic.

B0401.heard: Four lanes run under one playhead. A value track sets of properties such as rotation degrees to the key value at each moment. The top lane is the sword's rotation, ending at 75 degrees. A value track sets of property while a method track calls a function. For example, a spiked trap in your level could switch its visible property on and off with a value track.

B0402.heard: The second lane is a method track. It calls a function at chosen times here at 0.10 seconds to open the combo input buffer and at 0.25 seconds to allow the next swing. It does not fire when you scrub in the editor, only in a running game. For example, a door clip could call a function that unlocks the exit at the moment the door is fully open.

B0403.heard: The third lane is a Bezier track. It fills a value in between keys along a curve you shape by hand in the editor, not along a fixed rule. In this made-up curve, the value runs from zero up to one. For example, a camera that swoops into a boss room along a curve you have dragged into exactly the shape you want would use a Bezier track.

B0404.heard: The bottom lane is an audio track, it plays a sound stream at a chosen time in the clip. In this made up example, a woosh starts at 0.10 seconds and is still playing. For example, a sword attack in your game could carry its swing sound on an audio track, so the sound is timed by the clip itself and not by a separate script.

B0501.heard: Three graphs show where the playhead sits over six seconds for clip two seconds long. Loop mode is the setting for whether a clip plays once, loops, or ping pongs. At six seconds the play once clip has stopped at its end, the loop is back at zero and the ping pong is at its end again. Loop wraps from end to start and ping pong reverses at each end. For example, a walk cycle loops while a death animation plays once.

B0502.heard: Two loops of a walk cycle angle. A loop seam is a jump where the last value meets the first as a clip loops. In this made-up example, the upper loop ends at minus 10 degrees, so it jumps 20 degrees. The lower one ends at minus 30, where it began, so no seam. To test it, compare the value at zero and at length. For example, a run cycle whose last frame differs from its first makes the character hitch once every loop.

B0503.heard: Three bars race through one clip, 0.45 seconds long. Speed scale is a multiplier on how fast a clip plays, and the time to finish is the length divided by it. A speed scale of 0.5, the clip takes 0.9 seconds, and a 2 it takes 0.225. For example, a slow motion powerup could set the player character's animation player to a speed scale of 0.5, so attacks take twice as long.

B0601.heard: Two bars on a timeline of seconds after a scene loads. Autoplay names the animation a player starts by itself when it's seen loads. In this made-up example, the top clip starts at zero seconds. Without Autoplay, the lower clip waits for a script to call play here at 1.5 seconds. For example, a torch flickering on a dungeon wall is a good Autoplay clip, since it should run from the moment the level appears with no code.

B0602.heard: Now two clips end differently. Animation finished is the signal and animation player sends when a clip ends. The clip that plays once sends it at its end. A looping clip never ends so it never sends the signal. For example, your game over screen could wait for the death clip's animation finished signal, but if that clip were set to loop, the screen would never appear.

B0603.heard: Callback mode set when animation updates idle or physics and when method keys run, deferred or immediate. Here a key at 0.10 seconds at 120 frames per second falls on frame 12 on paper. Play leaves the playhead at 0 on the first frame and a deferred call waits for the frame to end so on the walker sword it was observed on frame 14, for example. A test asserting that your sword's method key fires on frame 12 would fail.

B0604.heard: Two graphs of one value, keyed zero, and then one at 0.15 seconds in this made up example. Update mode is set per value track. Continuous blends between keys so the upper line climbs. Discrete changes only at the keys so the lower line jumps. A yes or no value has nothing in between so it wants to scree. For example, when the Walker Sords hitbox was moved into its attack clips, it went on a discrete monitoring track. True and then falls.

B0701.heard: Three lines climb from a camera zoom of 1.0. A tween is a value animated from code toward a target, then thrown away. Its invaluable comes from gameplay, looked up at runtime. The gray animation always ends at 2.0, while tween A ends at 2.5 and tween B at 1.8 set by the player's target. For example, a health bar sliding down to whatever health the player has left is a tween.

B0702.heard: Four balls make the same trip in one second, easing is the speed curve of a change. Eason starts slow and ease out ends slow. At 0.25 seconds the Linnerball is 25% of the way, easing 6, ease out 44 and easing out 13. For example, a pause menu that moves in with ease out moves quickly at first, then settles gently into place.

B0703.heard: Six small graphs each in ease out curve. Transition type is the family of curve between follows, such as linear sine, cubic back bounce or elastic. Easing says which end is slow and the transition type says the shape. Back over shoots, reaching 1.09 at the halfway mark while bounce and elastic wobble to rest. For example, a coin that pops out of a block with the back type flies slightly past its spot before settling.

B0704.heard: One sword tween runs to the end and an identical one is stopped halfway. Kill a tween and it aborts where it is short of its end value and its final step never runs. Killed at 0.075 seconds the blade stays at 2.5 degrees and the hitbox stays on. So a gameplay fact like an active hitbox belongs in an animation. For example, a zoom tween killed when the player dies leaves the camera half zoomed.

B0801.heard: A two-bone arm, an upper arm, and a forearm. A skeleton is a hierarchy of bones where a child bone moves with its parent. Turn the upper arm to minus 50 degrees and the forearm set 70 degrees from it, rides along with the hand. Setting angles and then finding the hand like this is forward kinematics. For example, rotating only the thigh bone of a 2D character swings the shin and foot two because they are its children.

B0802.heard: A dashed straight arm appears beneath the bent one. The rest pose is the skeleton's default pose which you can return to at any time. Here every rest angle is zero, and the current pose sits minus 50 and 70 degrees away from it. Every animated pose is measured from rest. For example, an enemy whose arms are left bent after its attack clip can be reset to its rest pose before its next clip begins.

B0803.heard: Now the hand chases a moving target. Inverse kinematics or IK means you choose the target, and the solver computes the joint angles that reach it. For two bones, the law of cosines solves it. In this made up arm the target is 191 from the shoulder, of a reach of 280, and the angle at the elbow is 86 degrees. For example, in the walker IK build the mouse moves a target, and the robot's arms are solved to reach it.

B0804.heard: Two elbows, one up and one down, both reach the same target. A pole target is a helper point that sets which way an elbow or knee bends. Both solutions are correct, so only the pole can decide. Here the elbow goes down, the side near the pole. For example, a pole placed in front of a character's knee keeps the leg bending forward, never backwards.

B0901.heard: A three-bone chain is pulled to a target, pass by pass. Fabric forward and backward reaching inverse kinematics is an IK solver that moves the chain back from the target, then forward from the root, again and again, until it fits. And this made up chain the error falls from 255 pixels to 9.5 after four passes. For example, the Walker IK build use is a fabric plug-in written in GD script to pull a robot's arms toward the target.

B0902.heard: Both arms of a figure reach for one target. Skeleton IK3D is the older IK node built into Godot. Give it a bone chain and a target node and it solves the chain for you. Its class reference marks it deprecated, which means it may be changed or removed in a future version. For example, the Walker IK build runs Skeleton IK3D on both of the robot's arms and its check confirms that the solver is running.

B0903.heard: A single circle turns to face a target. Look at rotates one bone so it faces a target. No chain is solved, only one angle here minus 20 degrees. That is the difference from IK, which bends a whole chain. For example, a guard whose head bone turns to watch the player sneak past you's look at while reaching out with his arm would need IK.

B1001.heard: Two readings of the same arm taken at two moments. Skeleton updated is the signal a skeleton sends when its final pose I can include it is ready to read. Sampled after a timer the hand is still off the target because the IK has not been applied yet. Sampled in the signal it sits on the target. For example the Walker IK test first sampled the arms after a timer and passed 10 of 12 checks then sampled them in this signal and passed all 12.

B1002.heard: Four rows of frame ticks from a simulated run. A fixed frame rate set with the fixed FPS flag in a number makes every frame advance game timed by exactly one over that number in seconds. Pin the first frame at or past 0.1 seconds is frame 12 every time. Unpinned at drifts between 12 and 13. For example, the sword timing test written for Walker past 20 of 20 pinned and failed 7. 9 and 9 checks without the flag.

B1003.heard: A mouse mode request and a grid of eight checks. A back-end limit is something a headless run cannot test, such as a captured mouse, so it stays unverified, not passed. The Walker first-person scene asked for mouse mode two captured and got back zero visible. So four of its eight navigation checks fail and stay unverified. For example, if your game hides the cursor for mouse look, report that it is unverified until someone plays it in a real window.

B1101.heard: Each pair puts two lookalike ideas side by side. An animation is a clip with the end value in it, 1.0 every time and designers scrub it. A tween is computed in code toward a target from gameplay. Here's 0.8.

B1102.heard: Loop wraps from the end straight back to the start, so the playhead jumps. Ping Pong plays forward then backward and repeats so it never jumps. Only a loop needs its first and last values to match.

B1103.heard: Two bone IK is solved in one step with the law of cosines. Fabric repeats pass after pass until the chain fits the target here on pass 4 of 4. Two bones get an exact answer at once and a longer chain is solved by repeating.

B1104.heard: Continuous blends between keys, so a value climbs smoothly from one key to the next. Discrete changes only at the keys, so it holds, then jumps. Use discrete for anything that is simply on or off.

B1201.heard: Each vague request is turned into an exact instruction beside a chart of what it does. Make the swing slower becomes set speed scale to 0.5 on attack fast. 0.45 seconds becomes 0.9. Half speed doubles the time.

B1202.heard: Make the zoom feel smooth becomes between the zoom from 1.0 to 2.5 over 1 second with the quad transition type and ease out. At 0.25 seconds the zoom is already 1.66 against 1.38 for linear.

B1203.heard: Make the arm reach the target becomes 2-bone IK from shoulder to hand with a pole target above the elbow. At a target distance of 100 the elbow angle is 41 degrees and at 270 it is 149. A farther target means a straighter elbow.

B1204.heard: The hitbox should match the swing becomes key monitoring true at 0 seconds and false at 0.15 with update mode discrete. On paper that is frames 0 to 18 at 120 frames per second, observed frames 2 to 20, check frames not just seconds.

B1205.heard: Test the animation headless becomes run with the fixed FPS flag at 120 and read the pose in skeleton updated. Pinned the timing test failed none of its 20 checks. Unpinned the same test failed 7, 9 and 9. Pin the time step first.

B1301.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust a change to an animation. First, does a designer need to scrub it? Then it belongs in an animation. Does gameplay set the end value? Then it is a tween.

B1302.heard: Second, if the clip loops do its first and last values match, so there is no loop seam, and is the loop mode actually set?

B1303.heard: Third is every yes or no property, such as a hitbox's monitoring, keyed with update mode discrete, so it jumps at the key instead of blending.

B1304.heard: Fourth on which frame does the key really fire. The callback modes can move it, as the deferred call in the first frame after play did for the walker sword.

B1305.heard: Fifth, do you read the pose in the skeleton updated signal once the final pose with IK is ready and not after a timer which can look between updates.

B1306.heard: 6. Did you pin the time step and did you say what a headless run cannot test? Then say it exactly. Not make it smoother, but the quad transition ease out one second.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap, an animation is data, and an animation player is the node that plays it. A track binds one property and its keys are the points it passes through. A method track calls a function and it never fires while you scrub. A tween reads its end value from gameplay and can be killed halfway. Inverse kinematics sets the target and solves the angles and a poll picks the bend. Read the pose and skeleton updated and pin the time step before you test.

BHTF.heard: Give me short cases for making a game in Go-Doh one at a time, each showing an animation idea at work. Draw an animation player, track key, play head, method track, update mode, loop seam, tween, inverse kinematics and poll target. I answer with the exact term and say why it's look-alike does not fit. Wait for my answer before you reveal yours.

BOUT.heard: Key Terms Animation Foundations at Nick Bear Brown.
